l: Hippias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Hippias, brother of Thessalus and Hipparchus, is described as rigid and cruel. He ruled tyrannically over the Athenians with his brother.

l: Athenian tyranny, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Athenian tyranny is represented through the rigid and cruel rule of Hipparchus and Hippias, whose oppression led Harmodius and Aristogiton to conspire for the liberation of their country.

l: Zeno of Elea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Zeno of Elea was tortured after being seized for conspiring against the tyrant Nearchus. He endured the rack, then deceived Nearchus into approaching him and bit the tyrant's ear, refusing to release it until the guards begged him to do so.

l: Sextus Tarquinius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: assaults Lucretia [by threat and force at Collatia] Sextus Tarquinius went to Collatia and attempted to force Lucretia, threatening her with death and falsely framing her as an adulteress unless she yielded. He promised her rewards and marriage, but his violation led Lucretia to summon her household and take her own life.

l: Lucius Tarquinius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a king's nephew [husband of Lucretia] Lucius Tarquinius, the king's nephew, was Lucretia's husband. He was away with the army at Ardea when Sextus Tarquinius attacked her.

l: Lucretia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Lucretia was renowned for chastity and was attacked by Sextus Tarquinius while her husband was away. After Sextus left, she summoned her servants, denounced his violation of friendship and hospitality, and stabbed herself with a dagger.

l: suicide, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The unit describes Lucretia's suicide after Sextus Tarquinius violated her chastity, presenting her death as an act connected to her concern for honor.

l: Hippocrates of Gela, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Hippocrates of Gela rebuked the chief priests and citizens of Syracuse for plundering Jupiter's temple. He ordered them to return the sacred objects and did not take any of them himself, seeking both to preserve his reputation and to turn the people against Syracuse's oppressive governors.

l: Cimon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Cimon surrendered himself to imprisonment to pay his father's fine so that he could receive and bury his father's body. He later became a distinguished civil magistrate and a famous general, performing actions worthy of remembrance.

l: Dromichaetes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Dromichaetes, king of Thrace, rules Helis, captures Lysimachus, spares him, returns his companions, and uses a banquet to favor Macedonian supper.

l: capture of Lysimachus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Dromichaetes captured Lysimachus, king of Thrace, and treated him and his children with civility. He persuaded the Thracians to preserve Lysimachus and used his release and generous treatment to seek the restoration of Thracian forts and castles.

l: Timaeus's bias against Agathocles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a private pique [that corrupted historical writing] Timaeus’s hostility toward Agathocles arose after Agathocles banished him from Sicily. The text says that Timaeus invented accusations, reduced Agathocles’s successes, magnified his accidental misfortunes, and falsely portrayed a capable and courageous commander as a coward.

l: Xantippos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Xantippos, a Carthaginian ally, delivers the Carthaginians from immediate danger by routing the recently victorious Romans after great slaughter; his prudence, wisdom, and valour change the course of affairs and win widespread admiration.

l: peace between Rome and Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: A peace opportunity honourable to Romans but dishonourable to Carthaginians ends when Attilius Regulus rejects it and demands unreasonable conditions.

l: Attilius's defeat, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: causes Roman defeat by Xantippos Attilius's defeat followed his refusal to show clemency and humanity toward the distressed Carthaginians. His army was routed and cut off, and his resulting dishonour and disgrace outweighed his former glory and reputation.

l: sea-fights, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Sea-fights decide a conflict, destroying many Roman and allied ships and causing the deaths of one hundred thousand men.

l: the war between Rome and Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The war between Rome and Carthage lasts fifteen years, becoming the longest recorded from former times; after Rome's defeat by Xantippos, sea-fights decide it amid immense fleet expense.

l: Clodius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Clodius, hot-tempered, crack-brained, and contemptuous of others, took command at Lilybsum, blamed earlier consuls, rashly tried to block the harbor with a sea mole, and harshly punished soldiers and Roman allies.

l: Roman soldiers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Roman soldiers received a harsh commander in Clodius, who punished them severely and accused their former leaders of allowing them to indulge in wine, luxury, and pleasure.

l: siege of Lilybsum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The siege of Lilybsum was being conducted by a Roman army when Clodius arrived and assumed command. Clodius claimed that the Romans were more besieged than the enemy and attempted to block the harbor with a mole.

l: Amilcar (Carthaginian general), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Amilcar, a Carthaginian general, was known before appointment for magnanimity. As general he pursued fame, despised danger, and showed prudence, courage, and industry, becoming considered the best king and most valiant general before being imprisoned with Bostar's corpse.

l: hostages taken by Hanno, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: has_quantity three thousand Hanno took three thousand hostages after capturing Hecatompylos. The text later refers to captives who were confined and mistreated by the Attilius family.

l: Attilius's wife, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Attilius's wife, mother of his sons, grieves her husband's death, blames young men, and drives cruel punishment of captives, ordering her sons' harshness and imprisoning Amilcar with Bostar's corpse on scant food.

l: Attilius's sons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: confine the captives' confinement [in a little close room] Attilius's sons were urged by their mother to mistreat the captives because she believed their carelessness had caused their father's death. They confined the captives in a small room, where Bostar died after five days without food.

l: Bostar, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: dies_in the captives' confinement [after five days without meat, through vexation and famine] Bostar was one of the captives held in a cramped room by Attilius's sons. He died after five days without food from distress and starvation, and his body was later burned and his ashes sent back to his own country.

l: Attilii, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Attilii were held responsible for the cruel treatment of the captives and narrowly escaped being put to death. The magistrates threatened to punish them severely if they did not treat prisoners humanely in the future.

l: magistrates of Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: After tribunes report captives' mistreatment, magistrates summon and threaten the Attilii, blaming their mother; they arrange funerals for Bostar and Lucius iEmilius, send Bostar's ashes home, and free imprisoned Carthaginian general Amilcar.

l: Amilcar's imprisonment, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_in the captives' confinement [with Bostar's corpse] Amilcar was confined in a small, foul room with Bostar's corpse and was deprived of food except what was necessary to keep him alive. He prayed to Jupiter and the other gods for vengeance, but was eventually discovered and freed after servants reported his condition.

l: Bostar's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_caused_by famine [after five days without food] Bostar died after being confined without food for five days, overcome by mental anguish and famine. The magistrates had his body burned and sent the ashes back to his own country.

l: the captives' confinement, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The captives were thrust into a small enclosed room and forced to crowd together like beasts. They were kept without food for five days, resulting in Bostar's death, while Amilcar endured further confinement with the corpse until the authorities intervened.

l: mercenary soldiers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Mercenary soldiers, denied pay by Carthaginians, revolt, distress Carthage, and cruelly treat Carthaginian prisoners and confederates.

l: revolt of the mercenaries, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_caused_by mercenary soldiers [resentment of injury] The revolt began when the Carthaginians attempted to defraud their mercenary soldiers of their pay. It threatened the Carthaginians with the loss of both their sovereign authority and their country, and it was accompanied by severe cruelty on both sides.

l: Spondius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Spondius, a captain of the revolters, cruelly rejects burial and further messengers, orders captured Carthaginians killed, and mutilates captured confederates for return to Carthage.

l: war in Africa against the mercenaries and Libyans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_waged_in Africa The war in Africa involved the Carthaginians fighting the mercenaries and the Libyans, who had revolted and closely besieged Carthage itself. Amilcar performed notable actions in the war with great valor and prudence, and the war eventually ended.

l: Nabis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: sends_ambassadors_with Titus Quinctius Flamininus [to Rome concerning peace] Ambassadors from Nabis and Flamininus came to Rome concerning the terms of peace. The Senate confirmed the articles and ordered the removal of garrisons and the withdrawal of forces from Greece.

l: Hannibal's war in Italy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Hannibal's seventeen-year war in Italy was a campaign against powerful nations that wasted and harassed much of Italy, destroyed many cities, and depended on disciplined forces and stratagems. It unfolded through Hannibal's campaigns, disputes over captives and ambassadors, and ended with his return to Africa.

l: Hannibal's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Hannibal's army, comprising countrymen, foreigners, and mercenaries of varied temperaments and languages, obeys Hannibal and remains free of mutinies through his prudent conduct. Despite moving very large forces from place to place, it sustains orderly discipline and sufficient money and provisions.

l: battles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: are_won_by Hannibal [every battle he fought] Hannibal was victorious in every battle he fought in this account. His battles caused terrible slaughter among people reputed to be the leaders of the world, so that none dared face him or engage him in battle.

l: military discipline, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Military discipline in Hannibal's army was maintained through his prudent conduct, even though the soldiers differed in nationality, temperament, and language. The unit presents this discipline as a major reason he achieved greater and more renowned actions.

l: Tiberius Gracchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Tiberius Gracchus, a young lieutenant-general, distinguished himself in Spain through courage, prudence, and vigorous command. Later, as ambassador inspecting Syria, he was kindly received by Antiochus III without perceiving the king's hostile designs toward Rome. He was killed by Publius Scipio Nasica while allegedly seeking absolute monarchy; public anger subsided after Nasica admitted the killing and made that claim.

l: Paulus Æmilius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Paulus Æmilius, a Roman consul and general, was celebrated for nobility, prudence, courage, and military skill; in Macedonia he encouraged legions, used stratagems, defeated Macedonians, and mercifully treated Perseus.

l: Titus Quinctius Flamininus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: promotes_freedom_of Grecians [from garrisons and foreign government] Flamininus summoned the Greek nobility and explained that Greece would be free from garrisons and governed by its own laws, while asking that Italian servants be discharged. In negotiations with Antiochus, he presented the Roman alternatives concerning Antiochus's claims in Europe and Rome's support for its allies.

l: Scipio Africanus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Scipio Africanus is a Roman leader described as the most eminent of Romans before him. He conquered Hannibal and the Carthaginians, became adoptive grandfather of Publius Scipio, and later traveled as an ambassador through Alexandria, Egypt, Cyprus, Syria, and other regions, helping reconcile and judge disputes.

l: Roman conquest of Macedonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: results_in liberation of the Macedonian cities The Roman conquest of Macedonia followed many battles with Perseus and the overcoming of major dangers and difficulties. After gaining control of the country, the Romans proclaimed its cities free rather than reducing the population to perpetual slavery.

l: liberation of the Macedonian cities, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: After conquering Macedonia, the Romans proclaimed liberty to all its cities. This generosity exceeded what the conquered peoples had expected, since they believed their former injuries had left little room for mercy.

l: Battle with Perseus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Romans fought many battles against Perseus and overcame numerous dangers and difficulties before conquering Macedonia. Perseus's negligence, refusal to pay the Gauls, and other miscarriages contributed to the ruin of his kingdom.

l: Roman clemency toward defeated peoples, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Roman clemency toward defeated kings and peoples is presented as a policy that initially advanced Roman power through mercy. Under noble generals, Romans restored Antiochus and Philip, freed Macedonians, preserved Illyrian laws, and treated Perseus mildly. By making some conquered peoples friends, citizens, kin by marriage, or self-governing communities, they enlarged their dominion; later they mixed clemency with severity and destroyed cities to secure rule.

l: Asclepiades, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: governs city (governed by Asclepiades) [governor] Asclepiades, governor of the city, is brought while the accusations concerning the scheme and its victims are being made.

l: young man (Timotheus's persuaded accomplice), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: kills brother (the young man's brother) [impiously and unjustly] The young man is said to have been persuaded by Timotheus to kill his brother impiously and unjustly.

l: Philopater, surnamed Ariarathes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Philopater, surnamed Ariarathes, becomes king after his father's death, honors him with a splendid funeral, then welcomes friends, officers, commanders, and subjects, gaining universal goodwill.

l: Mithrobuzanes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_restored_to Mithrobuzanes's father's kingdom [by Ariarathes] Mithrobuzanes is restored by Ariarathes to his father's kingdom.

l: Artaxias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Artaxias, king of Armenia, rules while remaining covetous; after Antipater dies, he sends an ambassador to Ariarathes, urging the killing of a brother he holds and the division of Sophene.

l: Sophene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_proposed_to_be_divided_between Artaxias [and Ariarathes] Sophene is the territory that Artaxias proposes to divide with Ariarathes after they kill one of the brothers in his hands.

l: Mithrobuzanes's father's kingdom, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Mithrobuzanes's father's kingdom is restored to Mithrobuzanes by Ariarathes.

l: Antipater's death by torment, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Antipater's death occurs amid cruel torments, during which he accuses Timotheus of responsibility for the scheme.

l: Philopater's father's funeral, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_celebrated_with great pomp and state Philopater's father's funeral is celebrated with great pomp and state after Philopater comes to the crown.

l: Timotheus's design and contrivance, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Timotheus's design and contrivance are exposed when the great men and commanders begin to discover the whole scheme and pity those subjected to cruel torments.

l: the killing of the brother, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a killing The young man kills his brother after being persuaded by Timotheus; Artaxias later urges Ariarathes to participate in another killing of one of the brothers in his hands.

l: Ariarathes's restoration of Mithrobuzanes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Ariarathes, called Philopater, restores Mithrobuzanes to his father's kingdom through faithfulness and integrity, enabling Mithrobuzanes to regain it.

l: Publius Scipio, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Publius Scipio, natural son of Lucius iEmilius and adopted son of Scipio who conquered Hannibal and the Carthaginians, studied Greek learning from childhood and philosophy under Polybius from eighteen. After five years of struggle he attained habitual sobriety and temperance, and was noted for affability, generosity, chastity, courage, and hunting prowess beyond the Macedonian kings. As president of the council, he used inherited wealth generously: supporting Papiria, paying dowries immediately, giving money and inheritances to his brother and sisters, and helping fund funeral combats. When Antiochus offered his son's release and money for peace, Scipio refused the money and urged Antiochus not to resist the Romans.

l: funeral of Lucius iEmilius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: caused sorrow and lamentation [general, especially when the funeral was held] The funeral of Lucius iEmilius drew artificers, common people, the senate, magistrates, and people from neighboring free towns and cities. The widespread attendance reflected the general sorrow and lamentation caused by his death.

l: philosophy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Publius Scipio began studying philosophy at eighteen under Polybius of Megalopolis, the historian, who was his tutor. His study was associated with his growth in virtue and his distinction from those who had previously considered him dull and unworthy of his family.

l: sobriety and temperance, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Publius Scipio made sobriety his chief concern in youth and struggled against his natural lusts and the prevailing intemperance around him. Within five years he attained a fixed and habitual state of sobriety and temperance, which contributed to his reputation, health, and bodily strength.

l: generosity and liberality, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Publius Scipio displayed generosity and liberality by giving his inherited wealth to his mother, sisters, and brother, paying dowries immediately, and sharing the expense of his brother's funeral games. His reputation rested especially on choosing suitable opportunities and proper recipients for his gifts and benefits.

l: Orophernes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Orophernes, ruler of Cappadocia and brother of Ariarathes, deposes Ariarathes and rules through killings, payments, robbery, spoliation, and confiscation. He deposits four hundred talents with the Pirenians; as his affairs decline, he robs Jupiter’s temple to pay mercenary soldiers.

l: Demetrius of Syria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Demetrius of Syria, a king of the surviving royal stock, becomes increasingly cruel after the Romans conquer Perseus, urged by a flattering wicked friend. He kills opponents and Antiochians, burns Antioch, confiscates estates, drives citizens into exile, and is universally hated.

l: the Aradians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Aradians are a group that murder and plot against the Marathenians, then bribe Ammonius to surrender Marathos and violently reject Marathonian ambassadors' supplications before the senators imprison the ambassadors.

l: warfare and conquest, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The unit presents warfare and conquest as being secured both by force and by humane treatment. Philip son of Amyntas, Alexander son of Philip, and the Romans gained or maintained power through a mixture of military victories, clemency, and, when needed, the destruction of rebellious or hostile cities.

l: Ptolemy Physcon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Ptolemy Physcon is king of Egypt for fifteen years. Beginning by executing alleged plotters, banishing others on invented charges, and confiscating estates, he rules cruelly, receives Roman diplomatic gifts, and is hated by Egyptians; eventually Hierax takes over government amid threatened soldier revolt.

l: Diegylis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a king [of Thrace] Diegylis ruled his people tyrannically, treating them as slaves, plundering neighboring Greek cities, and committing many murders and abuses. His subjects hated him for his cruelty and covetousness, while Attalus gained praise by treating captives and refugees generously.

l: Numantians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Numantians sent four hundred soldiers to assist their countrymen in Lagnetia. When the Lagnetians planned to surrender them to Pompey, the Numantians attacked the citizens by night; after the city's capture, Pompey released the surviving Numantian auxiliaries.

l: Ptolemy Physcon's reign, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: has_duration fifteen years Ptolemy Physcon's reign began most wickedly with executions, torture, banishments, and confiscations. Despite the hatred these actions provoked, he reigned for fifteen years.

l: Viriathus's marriage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: At Viriathus's marriage, he mocked the displayed gold, silver, and rich carpets by holding them on a lance. He ate only bread and flesh, sacrificed according to the manner of the Spaniards, and carried his bride on horseback to his mountain apartments.

l: Siege of Lagnetia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: During Pompey's preparations to besiege Lagnetia, the Numantians sent four hundred soldiers to aid the city. The Lagnetians first welcomed and rewarded them but later sought terms with Pompey and considered surrendering their benefactors.

l: Capture of Lagnetia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Numantians attacked the Lagnetians after learning of the proposed betrayal. Pompey then scaled and captured the city, killed the Lagnetians, released the Numantians, and later razed the city.

l: Viriathus's burial, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Lusitanians buried Viriathus with great pomp and honor. Two hundred gladiators fought against two hundred others in single combats at his sepulchre.

l: Ptolemy's cruelty and tyranny, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Ptolemy's cruelty and tyranny included killing people on accusations of plots or invented crimes, banishing them, confiscating their estates, and ordering executions even during celebrations. His conduct caused his subjects to hate him and desire revolt.

l: Viriathus's virtues, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Viriathus was described as sober, temperate, honest, faithful to treaties, courageous, prudent, vigilant, and generous to his soldiers. He shared spoils without taking more than others, rewarded bravery, relieved the needy, and remained unconquered while commanding the Lusitanians.

l: Diegylis's atrocities, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: are_characterized_by unparalleled cruelty Diegylis's atrocities included torture, murder, rape, plunder, mutilation, crucifixion, and the dismemberment of captives and hostages. At his wedding he had two beautiful Greek brothers prepared as sacrificial victims, then killed both when the elder tried to protect the younger.

l: slave mutiny and sedition in Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: A slave rebellion in Sicily, sparked by masters' growing cruelty and slaves' hatred, became a vast mutiny. It ransacked cities, caused robbery, murder, insecurity, and the collapse of law and justice, while seeking masters' destruction. With no Roman praetor, lawlessness spread across the island, nearly placing Sicily under slave control.

l: rebellious slaves, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Rebellious slaves in Sicily suddenly unite against masters in large numbers, spreading violence through cities and countryside. Some become armed shepherds and herdsmen; others follow Eunus or Cleon. They devastate settlements, rob travelers and barns, seize herds, kill indiscriminately, and make highways impassable, while masters fear further urban revolt.

l: slaveholders and masters in Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: practice cruelty of masters toward slaves [increasing over time] Slaveholders bought whole gaols of prisoners to work their lands, overburdened them with labor, branded them, and often denied them adequate clothing, food, wages, and subsistence. Their cruelty and reliance on powerful connections prevented magistrates from punishing the slaves' abuses and helped produce the revolt.

l: Aristonicus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Aristonicus sought to gain the kingdom of Asia without any stated right. Slaves joined him because of their masters' cruelty, and together they filled many towns and cities with bloodshed.

l: Damophilus of Euna, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Damophilus of Euna is a wealthy landowner with extensive land and cattle. Proud and cruel, he imitates luxurious slaveholders, arms and displays slaves, entertains lavishly, and subjects captives to branding, fetters, imprisonment, hunger, inadequate clothing, and frequent scourging, provoking revolt.

l: luxury and moral corruption, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Luxury and moral corruption arise from excessive plenty: wealthy Sicily’s inhabitants become comfortable, indulgent, proud, and insolent, amid harsher masters and conditions for slave revolt. After conquest and peace, Rome likewise abandons military virtue for extravagance, wealth, and indulgence as happiness.

l: cruelty of masters toward slaves, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: contributes_to slave mutiny and sedition in Sicily [by provoking slave hatred] Cruelty by masters in Sicily increased steadily through branding, forced labor, inadequate food and clothing, withheld subsistence, imprisonment, and frequent scourging. The text presents this cruelty as a principal cause of the slaves' hatred and rebellion, and it likewise helped drive slaves in Asia to join Aristonicus.

l: slave labor and exploitation, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Slave labor and exploitation stigmatized purchased slaves, imposed severe agricultural and shepherding work without adequate support or wages, and culminated in armed shepherds becoming organized violent raiders.

l: Caius Gracchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Caius Gracchus was killed by the hands of his own servant. Lucius Vitellius cut off his head and brought it to Lucius Opimius in exchange for its weight in gold.

l: Adherbal, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Adherbal, king of Numidia and Rome’s ally, is Jugurtha’s brother; after defeat he flees to besieged Cirta, appeals unsuccessfully to Rome, and is killed with his children after its capture.

l: Metellus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_recalled_from banishment [by the Roman people] Metellus was restored from banishment after the Roman people were moved by the persistent appeals of his son. His recall was debated in public assemblies for two years.

l: Saturninus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Saturninus, a quaestor in Ostia, lived extravagantly and mismanaged grain transport to Rome, prompting the Senate to remove him. After becoming sober in conduct, he was chosen tribune of the people and opposed the Senate.

l: Quintus Mutius Scaevola, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Quintus Mutius Scaevola serves as proconsul in Asia, appoints Quintus Rutilius, and reforms corrupt practices through personal expense, moderation, justice, protection from oppression, suppression of false accusations, and punishment of abusive publicans.

l: Quintus Rutilius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Quintus Rutilius was chosen by Quintus Mutius Scaevola as his legate in Asia. Scaevola relied on his advice in administering the government and making laws.

l: publicans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: administer public administration and justice [at Rome and in the provinces] The publicans had filled Asia with oppression through illegal exactions and abuses. Quintus Mutius Scaevola restrained them, had injured people compensated, and imposed fines or death sentences for offenses according to their severity.

l: Roman knight Publius Rutilius Rufus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: advises Lucius Asellius [as counsellor in Syracuse] The Roman knight Publius Rutilius Rufus served as Lucius Asellius's counsellor in Sicily and resided at Syracuse. He was notable for piety toward the gods, sobriety and temperance, learning, courtesy, and generosity toward students of the liberal arts.

l: Lucius Asellius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Lucius Asellius, praetor in Sicily, finds the province devastated, appoints Caius Sempronius Longus, and with him and Publius Rutilius Rufus reforms administration, protects vulnerable people, suppresses injuries and false accusers, and restores prosperity.

l: Caius Sempronius Longus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Caius Sempronius Longus was chosen by Lucius Asellius as his legate in Sicily. He lived under the same roof as Asellius and joined him and Publius Rutilius Rufus in advising and judging the province.

l: Marcus Livius Drusus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Marcus Livius Drusus, a very young, eloquent, wealthy, courageous, and influential man, was praised for his qualities, faithful to his word, wealthier than the Roman people, and the senate's principal patron.

l: public administration and justice, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Public administration and justice were severely disordered in Sicily during the slave revolt, while provincial governors and tax collectors often oppressed the inhabitants. Quintus Mutius Scaevola and Lucius Asellius are presented as restoring justice through personal frugality, impartial judgments, protection of the weak, and punishment of abuses.

l: Metellus's recall from banishment, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Metellus's recall from banishment followed two years of public debate and the repeated pleas of his son, who appeared before citizens with unkempt hair and beard, tears in his eyes, and a torn garment. The Roman people granted the recall out of compassion despite concerns about violating the laws and setting a precedent.

l: Roman provincial reform, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_advanced_by Quintus Mutius Scaevola [through exemplary administration] Roman provincial reform is exemplified by Quintus Mutius Scaevola in Asia and Lucius Asellius in Sicily. Both relied on trusted advisers, paid their own expenses, resisted corruption and false accusations, protected the oppressed, and used justice and personal example to restore their provinces.

l: Caius Domitius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: counsels Pompoedius [to petition rather than attack the Senate] Caius Domitius met Pompoedius on the road and advised him to approach the Senate peacefully and respectfully. His prudent speech turned Pompoedius back and delivered Rome from threatened violence.

l: Cornelius Sylla, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_assigned Asia [as a province] Cornelius Sylla was assigned a province that Gaius Marius unlawfully sought to have transferred to himself. The text later describes Sylla as bringing a dreadful war upon Rome.

l: civil wars, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The civil wars in Rome enabled Gaius Marius to return after exile and join those judged enemies of the Romans. They produced proscriptions, murders of eminent men, the slaughter of much of the Senate, and the deaths of many soldiers.

l: Fimbria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Fimbria, a military leader, encouraged soldiers to plunder allies, seize captives, extort cities, and persecute Cyzicum, winning their loyalty through violence and retained wealth.

l: Albani, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Albani falsely accused the Romans of thefts and robberies and sent ambassadors to demand justice while threatening war. After Roman ambassadors were denied justice at Alba, the Albani became enemies of Rome.

l: war against Antiochus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Roman Senate prepared for the expected war against Antiochus by seeking Greek support and warning that it would aid its friends and allies. The conflict ended after Antiochus accepted severe Roman conditions and surrendered substantial territory, resources, and persons.

l: peace with Antiochus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Antiochus sought peace after abandoning thoughts of war and offered concessions, but the Romans required extensive territorial, financial, and military terms. Peace was granted after he accepted those conditions.

l: peace treaty with Antiochus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: A treaty requiring Antiochus to cede European and Taurus-side territories, surrender elephants and long ships, pay fifteen thousand Euboean talents, deliver named people, and provide Roman-chosen hostages.

l: Roman diplomatic embassies, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: are_received with courtesy [by the Roman Senate] Roman and foreign embassies addressed justice, alliances, peace, territorial claims, tribute, and military obligations. Roman representatives were sent to Alba, Asia, and other regions, while the Senate repeatedly received and judged ambassadors from Greece, Asia, Rhodes, and neighboring kingdoms.

l: Marathonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Marathonians refuse entrance to the king's soldiers after observing that the Aradians have greater favor with the king. They send ten eminent elders to Aradus with a supplication and sacred images, but the ambassadors are attacked and imprisoned.

l: Roman delegation to Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: inspects Egypt [including its cities, river, fortifications, and resources] The Roman delegation, including Scipio Africanus, inspects Alexandria, Egypt, Cyprus, Syria, and other regions. Its members prefer a spare and wholesome diet, disregard the king's luxury, and focus on strategic features; afterward they reconcile disputes, promote justice, renew leagues, and increase respect for Roman government.

l: Mark Antony, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: makes Cretan peace [with the Cretans] Mark Antony makes a peace with the Cretans, which they observe for some time. The later dispute between Rome and the Cretans concerns accusations against them and the terms of their relationship with Rome.

l: embassies, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Embassies in this unit present gifts, request alliances, negotiate peace, defend cities, surrender prisoners or hostages, and seek relief from Roman commands. Some are favorably received, while others are rejected, threatened, imprisoned, or dismissed after severe demands.

l: alliances and confederacies, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The senate breaks off its confederacy with the elder Ptolemy, expresses goodwill toward the younger Ptolemy, and recognizes Ariarathes's goodwill. It also restores or renews alliances with foreign peoples, initially declares the Cretans friends and confederates, and considers leagues involving Bocchus.

l: Roman treaties and commands, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: includes Cretan submission [surrender of ships, hostages, and tribute] Roman agreements and commands require submission, hostages, weapons, tribute, military assistance, or relocation. The Romans order the Carthaginians to surrender hostages and arms and leave Carthage, impose extensive conditions on the Numantians and Termissians, and command the Cretans to surrender ships, hostages, named individuals, and silver.

l: deserts of Susiana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: has water scarcity [for four hundred furlongs] The deserts of Susiana were entered by Alexander and his light-armed men during a night march. They had no apparent water for four hundred furlongs, and their heated sands produced a mist that made the plain seem like a vast ocean.

l: the river Oxus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The river Oxus is a destination reached by Alexander after desert marches, providing water for soldiers and those behind; during a later encampment nearby, springs of water and oil appeared near his pavilion.

l: water, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_used_by the two scouts [for their children] Water was scarce throughout the desert crossing, and some soldiers obtained small amounts through people familiar with the country. Two men brought water for their children in the army; one offered some to Alexander, but Alexander returned it and told him to give it to his children. After reaching the river Oxus, soldiers were ordered to carry water to their companions.

l: thirst and dehydration, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The lack of water and intense heat caused the soldiers’ mouths and entrails to become parched and made their spirits and bodies faint. Their thirst led some to consume wine or oil, while excessive drinking caused vomiting, loss of strength, and death.

l: Alexander's march through the desert, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: causes thirst and dehydration [through heat and lack of water] Alexander's march through the desert began at night and was more tolerable because of the dew and cool air. After sunrise, scorching heat and drought made the march grievous, and many soldiers suffered or fell behind before Alexander reached the river Oxus.

l: the Branchidae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Branchidae were a group removed from Miletus by Persian command to a distant little town after violating the Didymæus temple. Descended from Miletus’s betrayers, they spoke a mixed language and welcomed Alexander, who accepted their surrender, then killed them and destroyed their city for their ancestors’ betrayal.

l: little town of the Branchidae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The little town of the Branchidae was inhabited by people removed from Miletus by Xerxes. Alexander entered it with a select detachment while ordering the phalanx to surround its walls and raze it.

l: Milesians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Milesians, descended from Miletus, hated the Branchidae for ancestral betrayal; in Alexander’s army, Alexander left revenge or mercy to them, but they could not agree.

l: Didymæus temple, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Didymæus temple was described as a temple that the Branchidae had violated and whose contents they gave to Xerxes.

l: betrayal of Miletus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The betrayal of Miletus was attributed to the ancestors of the Branchidae, who had betrayed the Milesians and were associated with Xerxes. The descendants of the Branchidae were punished for this act even though many had never seen Miletus.

l: destruction of the Branchidae city, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: After the Branchidae surrendered, Alexander ordered their city razed: its walls were removed and sacred groves destroyed, leaving no sign.

l: the Branchidae massacre, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: kills the Branchidae [men, women, and children] The Branchidae massacre occurred after Alexander ordered the city surrounded and its inhabitants put to the sword. The disarmed Branchidae were killed indiscriminately, including men, women, and children, despite their prayers and entreaties.

l: Sogdians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Sogdians, people of Sogdia, repeatedly opposed Alexander. Many joined a defection after Bessos was seized; noble prisoners were spared and reportedly helped keep others obedient. They revolted again, refused Alexander’s governors, occupied forts and castles, fled to a steep rock, were defeated, and its defenders surrendered.

l: Asiatic Scythians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Asiatic Scythians, a Scythian people in Asia with an army, opposed Alexander at a river after hearing of revolt, but were defeated with heavy losses.

l: Spitamenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Spitamenes, a rebel leader, besieges Patachades' remaining garrison before fleeing to the Scythians as Alexander sends forces against him.

l: Cyropolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Cyropolis, the country’s greatest and largest city, built by Cyrus, had walls higher than the other seven cities and many barbarian soldiers. Alexander’s forces entered through its dry river channel, killed about eight thousand defenders, drove the rest into the castle, and compelled surrender after a day of thirst.

l: Iaxartes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a river [called Tanais in the narrative] The Iaxartes is identified in a note as the river called Tanais in the narrative. Alexander crossed it with his army and defeated the Scythians on the farther bank.

l: rebellion of the Sogdians and Bactrians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: A defection against Alexander by Sogdians, some Bactrians, and river-bordering barbarians. It began with surprise killings of Macedonian garrisons and fortified cities, expanded through occupied forts and rejected governors, and was reduced by Alexander's forces until remaining defenders surrendered after the rock's assault.

l: battle with the Scythians at the Iaxartes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a battle [between Alexander's forces and the Asiatic Scythians] Alexander first used engines to wound and frighten the Scythians across the narrow river, then crossed with his army. His cavalry and light-armed troops broke the Scythians’ formation and put them to flight, killing about a thousand and capturing one hundred and fifty, including Satrices.

l: siege of Cyropolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a siege [conducted by Alexander's forces] The siege began with orders to batter Cyropolis’s high walls using rams and other engines. Alexander then exploited the dry river channel to enter the city, after which the defenders fought fiercely before being driven from the marketplace and forced into the castle.

l: Scythian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Asiatic Scythian army at Tanais hurled darts and insulted Alexander, then resisted his cavalry before being surrounded, defeated, and forced to flee.

l: the seven cities of the country, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: A group of fortified cities in the country bordering Alexander's camp; barbarians fled there, and Alexander razed five in two days, then took Cyropolis after a siege and the seventh at first assault.

l: Maracanda, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The army's separate forces joined together at Maracanda after overrunning much of the country. From there Alexander sent Hephaestion to bring colonies into the cities of the Sogdians and ordered Coenus and Artabazus against the Scythians.

l: the rock, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The rock was steep and inaccessible on every side, and its defenders had stored provisions for a long siege. Macedonians climbed it at night using crampons and cords, and the defenders surrendered after seeing soldiers on its summit.

l: assault on the rock, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander ordered an assault on the rock after the defenders rejected his offer of safe return and mocked his ability to take it. The Macedonian climbers reached the summit, despite about thirty deaths, and their appearance led the defenders to surrender.

l: surrender of the defenders, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The defenders surrendered when they saw Macedonian soldiers on the summit and mistakenly believed that the force was larger and better armed than it was. Many wives and children were taken prisoner, including Oxyartes's wife and daughters and his nine-year-old son.

l: Bahastis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: contains the wild beasts of Bahastis [in large woods and forests] Bahastis is described as having a multitude of stately wild beasts ranging through large woods and forests. Its woods are spacious, watered by many springs, enclosed by walls, and furnished with towers from which hunts could be viewed.

l: Bazaria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Bazaria is a country with frequent, spacious forests, where Alexander came and hunted a chase untouched for four generations.

l: hunting, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The hunting took place in spacious, enclosed woods supplied with springs and viewing towers. A hunting ground that had been untouched for four generations was opened, and four thousand wild beasts were killed while Alexander's army was in the forest.

l: the wild beasts of Bahastis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The wild beasts of Bahastis are presented as evidence of the riches of the barbarians in those places. They were numerous and included stately beasts living in extensive woods and forests.

l: the lion that attacked Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: A vast lion attacks Alexander during a hunt in Bazaria; Alexander stops Lysimachus and kills it with one blow.

l: the Macedonian decree concerning Alexander's hunting, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: After Alexander is delivered from a lion, the Macedonians establish a customary decree requiring guards of captains and friends whenever he hunts on foot.

l: the lion hunt in Bazaria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: includes Alexander's army [hunting in the forest] During the lion hunt in Bazaria, Alexander's army entered a chase that had been untouched for four generations and drove out the game. A huge lion attacked Alexander, and Alexander killed it after Lysimachus attempted to assist.

l: the death of Clitus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Clitus died after Alexander, overcome by anger and drunkenness, ran him through with a weapon. Accounts differ on whether Alexander used a lance taken from a guard or a sarissa, and Aristobulus gives a version in which Clitus returned after initially escaping.

l: Alexander's killing of Clitus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a killing [committed by Alexander] Alexander killed Clitus during a drunken quarrel after Clitus reproached him and praised Philip. The text condemns Alexander's conduct as arising from anger and drunkenness, though it also says that Clitus's insolence was blameworthy.

l: the sacrifice to Bacchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a religious sacrifice [performed by Alexander after Clitus's death] After Clitus's death, Alexander's friends persuaded him to eat and drink, and he eventually sacrificed to Bacchus. The sacrifice followed the priests' claim that Bacchus was responsible for the misfortune resulting from Alexander's earlier neglect.

l: Alexander's remorse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander immediately regretted killing Clitus and reportedly tried to take his own life by setting a spear against a wall. He lay on his bed calling Clitus's name, declared himself the murderer of his friends, and refused food or drink for three days while neglecting himself.

l: Anaxarchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Anaxarchus, a sophist, argues that Alexander deserves divine honors more than Bacchus or Hercules and should be worshipped while alive, provoking Callisthenes’ rebuke.

l: Hermolaus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Hermolaus, son of Sopolides, is a Macedonian nobleman's son, king's attendant youth, and student of Callisthenes. Disgraced after killing a boar before Alexander, he joins and recruits Sostrates for a conspiracy against Alexander, confesses when captured, and is stoned to death.

l: page corps, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The page corps consists of sons of Macedonian nobility serving Alexander as body squires and bedchamber attendants, receiving his horses, helping him mount, and accompanying hunts before some join a conspiracy to kill him asleep.

l: divine honors, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: are_distinct_from human honors [Callisthenes argues that the two forms of honor must not be confused] The text distinguishes divine honors from human honors by associating them with temples, sacrifices, drink offerings, hymns, dancing, and adoration. Callisthenes argues that Alexander may deserve the greatest human honors but should not assume or accept divine honors.

l: adoration of Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_opposed_by Callisthenes [because it gives a mortal divine honors] Anaxarchus advocates the adoration of Alexander, and Alexander sends men to urge the Macedonians to remember this practice. Eminent Persians rise and adore Alexander; in another account, participants drink from a golden bowl and then prostrate themselves and kiss him. Callisthenes drinks but refuses to adore Alexander, after which Alexander turns away from him.

l: pages' conspiracy against Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Hermolaus, Sostrates, and other royal pages plot to kill Alexander in his sleep after Hermolaus is humiliated. Alexander stays awake, the attempt fails, and Epimenes’s disclosure leads to the conspirators’ arrest, interrogation, and confession.

l: death of Callisthenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a reported death [the sources disagree whether he was hanged or died in chains] The unit reports conflicting accounts of the death of Callisthenes. Aristobulus says that he was carried about with the army in chains and died, while Ptolemy says that he was first racked and then hanged. The text presents these accounts after explaining that Callisthenes was accused of involvement in the pages' conspiracy.

l: the king's expedition against the Nauticans, or Nomvans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The king's expedition against the Nauticans, or Nomvans, marched from winter-quarters toward Gabazat until a violent third-day storm disrupted it and caused extensive loss of life.

l: the storm, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: A violent, severe storm develops over several days, culminating in continual lightning and thunder, then violent hail; darkness overwhelms the army before it somewhat abates.

l: hail, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_frozen_by the cold [during the storm] The hail fell with such violence that the soldiers covered themselves with their shields and then dropped their arms when their hands became numb and frozen. The cold froze the hail as many soldiers lay or wandered in the woods.

l: the cold, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The cold, intense and persistent, overcame soldiers’ natural heat, left many immovable, caused deaths, while fires gradually revived some survivors.

l: the destruction of the army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_caused_by the storm [a great storm] The destruction caused by the storm and cold swept away a thousand soldiers and other mean attendants upon the camp. Some of the dead were reportedly found standing beside trees in the same postures they had held when they died.

l: marriage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander married Roxana and induced many of his friends to marry the daughters of chief men among the barbarians.

l: Alexander's falling in love with Roxana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a love [deep] Alexander fell deeply in love with Roxana upon seeing her. He would not use her dishonourably as a captive and took her for his wife.

l: Peucelaotis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Peucelaotis was the country into which Hephaestion and Perdiccas were sent with troops to take the towns by force or persuasion and prepare for crossing the Indus.

l: Astes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: governs Peucelaotis [governor of the country before his revolt] Astes, the governor of Peucelaotis, attempted to revolt and withdrew into a city. Hephaestion besieged and captured it after thirty days, and Astes was killed.

l: first city attacked by Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: A city, first attacked during the advance, resisted Alexander’s initial advance; its outer then inner walls fell, defenders fled toward the mountains, and the city was leveled.

l: the siege of Astes's city, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: lasts thirty days The siege of Astes's city lasted thirty days and was conducted by Hephaestion. The city was captured, Astes was killed, and Sangius was made its governor.

l: Alexander's assault on the first city, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a assault [against the first city attacked by Alexander] Alexander's assault began when he defeated the defenders outside the first city and drove them inside. He was slightly wounded in the shoulder by a dart, then encamped against a suitable section of the wall; the Macedonians captured the outer wall the following morning and later scaled the inner wall.

l: massacre of the prisoners, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a massacre [of prisoners taken in the first city attacked by Alexander] After the first city fell, the prisoners were put to the sword because Alexander had been wounded. Many inhabitants who fled toward the nearby mountains were also killed during the pursuit.

l: Nysa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Nysa is a city between Cophlas and the Indus, said to have been founded by Bacchus for unfit soldiers descended from his family and named from his nurse. It governed itself aristocratically, supplied Alexander three hundred horsemen, and retained freedom after his grant; ivy uniquely grew there in India.

l: Acuphis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Acuphis, chief man of Nysa, led its delegation to Alexander, secured the city's freedom and its leading men, and became governor of Nysaea.

l: Nysaea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_named_after Nysa [the country was called Nysaea] Nysaea was the country associated with Nysa. Alexander made Acuphis governor of the whole province of Nysaea.

l: Meros, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Meros is a mountain overlooking Nysa, named for a thigh because Bacchus was fabled cherished in his father's thigh; Alexander later visited its ivy, laurel, and shady groves.

l: Nysaeans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Nysaeans, a free people inhabiting Nysa, send Acuphis and thirty leaders to Alexander, who lets them remain self-governing under their own laws.

l: the aristocracy of Nysa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Nysa's aristocracy, three hundred horsemen, governed the city; Alexander demanded one hundred members, but abandoned the demand after Acuphis's argument.

l: Nysa's laws, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: govern Nysaeans [according to their own laws] Nysa's laws allowed the city to be governed under an aristocracy. Alexander learned of this constitution, commended it, and allowed the Nysaeans to continue governing according to their own laws.

l: Dionysius's Indian expedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Dionysius's Indian expedition was described as a conquest of the Indians followed by a return toward the Grecian sea. The expedition was said to have led to the foundation of Nysa as a memorial of his victory.

l: Alexander's arrival at Nysa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander arrives at Nysa with his army; Acuphis and thirty leading men request the city remain free, and he grants it.

l: Nysa's foundation, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Nysa's foundation is a city foundation attributed to Bacchus, built for his war-unserviceable soldiers, named after his nurse, and commemorating Dionysius's Indian expedition as a perpetual monument.

l: ivy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: grows_in Nysa [the Nysaeans present this as proof of Bacchus's foundation] Ivy was said to grow nowhere in India except at Nysa, which the Nysaeans offered as evidence that Bacchus had founded the city. Alexander and the Macedonians viewed the ivy on Mount Meros, and some of it was used to crown their heads while they sang praises to Bacchus.

l: Massaga, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Massaga, the country’s greatest strong city, was defended by seven thousand mercenary Indians until its defenders were killed or withdrew; Alexander then captured it by storm and took the mother and daughter of Assacenus.

l: barbarians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Barbarians, an army dispersed among cities, join mercenary Indians defending Massaga against Macedonians, fight fiercely, and are driven back into the city.

l: mercenary Indians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Seven thousand valiant mercenary Indians entered Massaga to aid its defenders and fought Alexander fiercely. After losses and the governor's death, they agreed to join him but planned to flee rather than fight other Indians. Alexander surrounded their hill camp at night and killed them all.

l: Massaga siege, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Massaga was a four-day siege in which Macedonians used engines, a wooden tower, bridges, archers, and assaults until the governor’s death weakened defenders; Alexander captured it by storm, with twenty-five Macedonians killed.

l: execution of the mercenary Indians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Execution of mercenary Indians: after agreeing to join Alexander, surviving members camped separately and prepared to flee; Alexander surrounded their hill and put every one to the sword.

l: Cyrus the Younger, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_routed_by Artaxerxes II [in the war for the Persian throne] Cyrus fought his brother Artaxerxes for the Persian throne. He was routed, and the Greek forces that had served him made a long and difficult march out of Persia.

l: Philip II of Macedon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_hostage_at Thebes [before escaping and becoming king of Macedon] Philip escaped from hostagehood at Thebes, defeated the Athenians, subdued the Paeonians, and routed the Illyrians. He took Amphipolis, Olynthus, Elatea, and other cities, raised the siege of Byzantium after Athenian intervention, defeated the Athenians at Chaeronea, and was made general of Greece before being murdered.

l: Sicilian wars, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Sicilian wars included Dionysius's struggles against the Syracusans, Rhegium, and the Carthaginians, as well as the later conflicts involving Dionysius the Younger, Dion, Hicetas, and Timoleon. Timoleon ultimately defeated the Carthaginians and restored order in Sicily.

l: Book XVIII, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Book XVIII recounts succession after Alexander’s death: Arrhidaeus’s appointment, provincial division, Greek revolt and Lamian War, Perdiccas’s Egypt invasion, Antigonus-Eumenes struggles, and Cassander’s rise.

l: Book XIX, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a book It follows Antigonus’s campaigns against Eumenes and his rivals, the consolidation of Cassander’s power, and the activities of Ptolemy, Seleucus, Lysimachus, and Demetrius. It also describes conflicts in Macedonia, Greece, Asia, Sicily, and Italy.

l: Rhodes siege, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a siege [of Rhodes by Demetrius] The siege of Rhodes by Demetrius continues before peace is made with the Rhodians. The unit also records the actions of the Rhodian sea-captains during the siege.

l: The Aeneid
s: Helenus speaks these words (from his mouth divine)
q: Then, with his god possess’d, before the shrine, These words proceeded from his mouth divine:

l: The Aeneid
s: Anchises is honored by Venus (favored by divine love)
q: Old happy man, the care of gods above, Whom heav’nly Venus honour’d with her love,

l: The Aeneid
s: Andromache is a queen (Trojan queen at Epirus)
q: Nor less the queen our parting thence deplor’d, Nor was less bounteous than her Trojan lord.

l: The Aeneid
s: Andromache is widow of Hector (she identifies herself as Hector’s wife)
q: Accept,’ she said, ‘these monuments of love, Which in my youth with happier hands I wove: Regard these trifles for the giver’s sake; ’Tis the last present Hector’s wife can make.

l: The Aeneid
s: Ascanius is son of Aeneas (young Trojan son)
q: A noble present to my son she brought, A robe with flow’rs on golden tissue wrought,

l: The Aeneid
s: Ascanius resembles Astyanax (in features, form, eyes, motions, and frame)
q: Thou call’st my lost Astyanax to mind; In thee his features and his form I find: His eyes so sparkled with a lively flame; Such were his motions; such was all his frame;

l: The Aeneid
s: Achaemenides is a Greek from Ithaca (abandoned survivor of the Cyclops’ cave)
q: From Ithaca, my native soil, I came To Troy; and Achaemenides my name.

l: The Aeneid
s: Achaemenides is abandoned in the Cyclops’ cave (left behind by Ulysses’s companions)
q: Me my poor father with Ulysses sent; (O had I stay’d, with poverty content!) But, fearful for themselves, my countrymen Left me forsaken in the Cyclops’ den.

l: The Aeneid
s: Polyphemus is a monstrous host (more than human size)
q: Our monstrous host, of more than human size, Erects his head, and stares within the skies;

l: The Aeneid
s: Polyphemus has one eye (in the middle of his forehead)
q: Beneath his frowning forehead lay his eye; For only one did the vast frame supply;

l: The Aeneid
s: Helenus serves Phoebus (as a prophetic priest)
q: To Phoebus, next, my trembling steps he led, Full of religious doubts and awful dread.

l: The Aeneid
s: Polyphemus eats human flesh (with human blood as wine)
q: The joints of slaughter’d wretches are his food; And for his wine he quaffs the streaming blood.

l: The Aeneid
s: the blinding of Polyphemus bears their fate (not unrevenged)
q: Not unreveng’d Ulysses bore their fate, Nor thoughtless of his own unhappy state;

l: The Aeneid
s: the Cyclops’ cave is a large dark cave (paved with the remains of victims)
q: The cave, tho’ large, was dark; the dismal floor Was pav’d with mangled limbs and putrid gore.

l: The Aeneid
s: Phoebus assists the Trojans (according to Helenus’s prophecy)
q: Nor let the threaten’d famine fright thy mind, For Phoebus will assist, and Fate the way will find.

l: The Aeneid
s: Juno is a mighty queen (requiring vows, gifts, and prayers)
q: Above the rest, great Juno’s name adore; Pay vows to Juno; Juno’s aid implore. Let gifts be to the mighty queen design’d, And mollify with pray’rs her haughty mind.

l: The Aeneid
s: the Trojans inherits these rites and customs (to your pious race)
q: These rites and customs to the rest commend, That to your pious race they may descend.

l: The Aeneid
s: the Trojans are forbidden to land at Epirus (because the coast is held by Greek enemies)
q: Let not thy course to that ill coast be bent, Which fronts from far th’ Epirian continent: Those parts are all by Grecian foes possess’d;

l: The Aeneid
s: the Greeks possess Epirus (as hostile occupants)
q: Those parts are all by Grecian foes possess’d;

l: The Aeneid
s: Italy is seen the hills and plains (from far)
q: And now the rising morn with rosy light Adorns the skies, and puts the stars to flight; When we from far, like bluish mists, descry The hills, and then the plains, of Italy.

l: The Aeneid
s: Helenus’s prophecy concerns Aeneas’s voyage (guidance for Aeneas)
q: Of many things some few I shall explain, Teach thee to shun the dangers of the main, And how at length the promis’d shore to gain.

l: The Aeneid
s: Troy is the origin of the Trojans (ancestral homeland)
q: As both of us our birth from Troy derive,

l: The Aeneid
s: the Trojan state is founded by Aeneas (in Italy by force of arms)
q: Now part in peace; pursue thy better fate, And raise, by strength of arms, the Trojan state.’

l: The Aeneid
s: the straits of Messina separate Italy (from Sicily)
q: Th’ Italian shore And fair Sicilia’s coast were one, before An earthquake caus’d the flaw: the roaring tides The passage broke that land from land divides;

l: The Aeneid
s: Scylla is a sea monster (with a human face, virgin bosom, and dog-like lower parts)
q: But Scylla from her den, with open jaws, The sinking vessel in her eddy draws, Then dashes on the rocks. A human face, And virgin bosom, hides her tail’s disgrace: Her parts obscene below the waves descend, With dogs inclos’d, and in a dolphin end.

l: The Aeneid
s: Charybdis is a greedy whirlpool
q: Charybdis roaring on the left presides, And in her greedy whirlpool sucks the tides; Then spouts them from below: with fury driv’n, The waves mount up and wash the face of heav’n.

l: The Aeneid
s: Cumae contains Sibyl of Cumae (in a cave near Avernus)
q: Arriv’d at Cumae, when you view the flood Of black Avernus, and the sounding wood, The mad prophetic Sibyl you shall find, Dark in a cave, and on a rock reclin’d.

l: The Aeneid
s: Sibyl of Cumae is a prophetess (mad and prophetic)
q: The mad prophetic Sibyl you shall find, Dark in a cave, and on a rock reclin’d.

l: The Aeneid
s: Sibyl of Cumae writes on the Sibyl’s leaves (her prophecies and fates)
q: She sings the fates, and, in her frantic fits, The notes and names, inscrib’d, to leafs commits.

l: The Aeneid
s: Mount Etna emits hot embers (from her entrails)
q: By turns a pitchy cloud she rolls on high; By turns hot embers from her entrails fly, And flakes of mounting flames, that lick the sky. Oft from her bowels massy rocks are thrown, And, shiver’d by the force, come piecemeal down. Oft liquid lakes of burning sulphur flow, Fed from the fiery springs that boil below.

l: The Aeneid
s: Helenus’s prophecy foretells the sow omen (as a sign of the future settlement)
q: When, in the shady shelter of a wood, And near the margin of a gentle flood, Thou shalt behold a sow upon the ground, With thirty sucking young encompass’d round; The dam and offspring white as falling snow: These on thy city shall their name bestow, And there shall end thy labours and thy woe.

l: The Aeneid
s: Enceladus lies beneath Mount Etna (mythic explanation for the volcano)
q: Enceladus, they say, transfix’d by Jove, With blasted limbs came tumbling from above; And, where he fell, th’ avenging father drew This flaming hill, and on his body threw.

l: The Aeneid
s: Drepanum receives the Trojan fleet (as the port where Anchises dies)
q: At length on shore the weary fleet arriv’d, Which Drepanum’s unhappy port receiv’d.

l: The Aeneid
s: the gods cares for Old happy man (of gods above)
q: Old happy man, the care of gods above,

l: The Aeneid
s: Palinurus is wakeful (to spy the face of heav’n and the nocturnal sky)
q: Then wakeful Palinurus rose, to spy The face of heav’n, and the nocturnal sky;

l: The Aeneid
s: the famine prophecy is negated by Phoebus (divine assistance prevents the threatened famine)
q: Nor let the threaten’d famine fright thy mind, For Phoebus will assist, and Fate the way will find.

l: The Aeneid
s: Aeneas is a goddess-born leader (protected by Jove and directed by fate)
q: O goddess-born, (for Heav’n’s appointed will, With greater auspices of good than ill, Foreshows thy voyage, and thy course directs; Thy fates conspire, and Jove himself protects,)

l: The Aeneid
s: Aeneas is son of Anchises (Trojan family relationship)
q: If ever I ascend the Latian throne, And build a city I may call my own; As both of us our birth from Troy derive,

l: The Aeneid
s: Dido is a queen (of Carthage)
q: But anxious cares already seiz’d the queen:

l: The Aeneid
s: Aeneas is a Trojan prince (and hero)
q: The queen, Aeneas, and the Tyrian court Shall to the shady woods, for sylvan game, resort.

l: The Aeneid
s: Aeneas is a son of Venus (as described by Jupiter)
q: Not so fair Venus hop’d, when twice she won Thy life with pray’rs, nor promis’d such a son.

l: The Aeneid
s: Aeneas is destined to found Rome (through his descendants)
q: Hers was a hero, destin’d to command A martial race, and rule the Latian land, Who should his ancient line from Teucer draw, And on the conquer’d world impose the law.’

l: The Aeneid
s: Aeneas is destined for Latium (as the land he must reach)
q: Nor future praise from fading pleasure wean, Yet why should he defraud his son of fame, And grudge the Romans their immortal name! What are his vain designs! what hopes he more From his long ling’ring on a hostile shore, Regardless to redeem his honour lost, And for his race to gain th’ Ausonian coast!

l: The Aeneid
s: Aeneas loves Dido (in a cave union arranged by the gods)
q: The queen and prince, as love or fortune guides, One common cavern in her bosom hides.

l: The Aeneid
s: Aeneas possesses Dido's gift (a purple scarf and jeweled sword while in Carthage)
q: A purple scarf, with gold embroider’d o’er, (Queen Dido’s gift,) about his waist he wore; A sword, with glitt’ring gems diversified, For ornament, not use, hung idly by his side.

l: The Aeneid
s: Ascanius is a son of Aeneas (the heir whose future is invoked)
q: Regard the fortunes of thy rising heir: The promis’d crown let young Ascanius wear, To whom th’ Ausonian scepter, and the state Of Rome’s imperial name is ow’d by fate.”

l: The Aeneid
s: Juno is a goddess (who governs marriage)
q: Preferring Juno’s pow’r, for Juno ties The nuptial knot and makes the marriage joys.

l: The Aeneid
s: Juno governs marriage (as the deity who ties the nuptial knot)
q: Preferring Juno’s pow’r, for Juno ties The nuptial knot and makes the marriage joys.

l: The Aeneid
s: Venus descries hidden fraud (artfully)
q: Then Venus, who her hidden fraud descried, Which would the scepter of the world misguide To Libyan shores, thus artfully replied:

l: The Aeneid
s: Venus is mother of Aeneas
q: Not so fair Venus hop’d, when twice she won Thy life with pray’rs, nor promis’d such a son.

l: The Aeneid
s: Jupiter is a supreme god (ruler of heaven and earth)
q: All-pow’rful Jove, Who sways the world below and heav’n above, Has sent me down with this severe command:

l: The Aeneid
s: Jupiter commands Mercury (to order Aeneas to leave Carthage)
q: He calls Cyllenius, and the god attends, By whom his menacing command he sends: “Go, mount the western winds, and cleave the sky; Then, with a swift descent, to Carthage fly:

l: The Aeneid
s: Mercury is a messenger of Jupiter (divine messenger)
q: He calls Cyllenius, and the god attends, By whom his menacing command he sends:

l: The Aeneid
s: Mercury possesses Mercury's magic wand (a symbol of sovereign power)
q: But first he grasps within his awful hand The mark of sov’reign pow’r, his magic wand;

l: The Aeneid
s: Fate assigns Rome (to Ascanius and his descendants)
q: The promis’d crown let young Ascanius wear, To whom th’ Ausonian scepter, and the state Of Rome’s imperial name is ow’d by fate.”

l: The Aeneid
s: Cupid is a god (a soft god who inflames Dido)
q: A gentle fire she feeds within her veins, Where the soft god secure in silence reigns.

l: The Aeneid
s: Fame is a monstrous phantom (winged and many-tongued)
q: Swift is her walk, more swift her winged haste: A monstrous phantom, horrible and vast. As many plumes as raise her lofty flight, So many piercing eyes inlarge her sight; Millions of opening mouths to Fame belong, And ev’ry mouth is furnish’d with a tongue, And round with list’ning ears the flying plague is hung.
